name: Labrang

local_name.name: Labrang (also Palden Phuntshog Phodrang)
local_name.meaning: Labrang means 'lama's dwelling'; the monastery is also known as Palden Phuntshog Phodrang

tagline: A Nyingma monastery above Phodong with its original timber frame
meta_description: Labrang Monastery near Phodong: Nyingma, built 1826 to 1843, 2 km above Phodong Monastery. Altitude about 7,000 ft, its museum, permits, costs and tips.
summary: Labrang Monastery is a Nyingma monastery about 2 km above Phodong Monastery and 38 km from Gangtok, at roughly 7,000 ft (2,130 m) according to Sikkim Tourism. Wikipedia records it as built from 1826 to 1843 and still holding its original timber structure. It lies below the protected areas, so Indian visitors need no permit.
intro: Labrang Monastery stands on a flat ledge in forest about 2 km above Phodong Monastery, 38 km from Gangtok. Sikkim Tourism gives its altitude as about 7,000 ft, or roughly 2,130 m, which is why the air is cooler than in the town below. The name means lama's dwelling, and the monastery is also called Palden Phuntshog Phodrang.

Wikipedia records that Labrang was built from 1826 to 1843 by Gyalshe Rigzing Chempa, a son of Chogyal Tsugphud Namgyal, in memory of Lhatsun Chempo, the Tibetan lama associated with the Nyingma order in Sikkim. It was renovated with government aid in 1978 and damaged in the 2006 earthquake. The article says that the building keeps its original structure, whereas similar buildings elsewhere in Sikkim have burned down.

Inside are statues, texts and murals, with a museum collection of Buddha figures and sutras and a bronze statue of Karma Guru, a wrathful form of Padmasambhava. Labrang is quieter than Phodong, with fewer visitors and more forest. Indian visitors need no protected area permit, and the road up is short and steep. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: A monastery built in memory of Lhatsun Chempo
story.text: Wikipedia's article on Labrang Monastery (Sikkim), citing the Sikkim Tourism Development Corporation and the state's Ecclesiastical Affairs Department, says the monastery was built from 1826 to 1843 by Gyalshe Rigzing Chempa, son of Chogyal Tsugphud Namgyal. It was built in memory of Lhatsun Chempo of Kongpo in Tibet, the Nyingma lama who in Sikkimese tradition took part in the 1642 consecration of the first Chogyal at Yuksom. That connection is told in Sikkimese histories and on Wikipedia's Kabi Lungchok page and is not documented in the Labrang article, so we mark it as tradition. The article also says a major renovation took place in 1978 with government aid, and that the monastery was damaged in the 2006 earthquake. Its structure of wooden pillars and roofing has since been reinforced with steel. Where similar buildings in Sikkim have burned down, Labrang is said to have kept its original frame. We have not found a founding story beyond these written sources.
story.source: Wikipedia, Labrang Monastery (Sikkim); Sikkim Tourism Development Corporation

little_known.fact: Labrang translates as 'lama's dwelling', and the monastery is also known as Palden Phuntshog Phodrang or Palden Phuntsok Monastery.
Its wooden pillars and roofing have been reinforced with steel, and the building is described as keeping its original structure while similar buildings in Sikkim have burned down.
The monastery holds a bronze statue of Karma Guru, a wrathful form of Padmasambhava, and a museum with Buddha statues, sutras and murals.

facts: Nyingma monastery, museum, original timber structure
Not needed for Indian visitors; foreigners need the Sikkim restricted area permit

highlights.title: A Nyingma monastery
highlights.text: Labrang belongs to the Nyingma order, the oldest of the Tibetan Buddhist schools. Unlike Phodong, which is Kagyu, it gives you a second tradition in one outing. Remove shoes and hats before entering, and ask before photographing inside.

highlights.title: The museum collection
highlights.text: Wikipedia records a museum with a large collection of Buddha statues, sutras and murals. Opening hours depend on the monastery, so check current status. If it is closed, the prayer hall and courtyard are still worth a visit.

highlights.title: Karma Guru statue
highlights.text: The bronze statue of Karma Guru, a wrathful form of Padmasambhava, is among the notable objects. Ask a monk or caretaker about the meaning of the form if the opportunity arises, and do not touch statues.

highlights.title: A forest ledge at 2,130 m
highlights.text: The monastery stands on flat ground on a hill in dense forest, around 7,000 ft by Sikkim Tourism's figure. Mist moves through the trees in the afternoon and the air is cool, so carry a jacket even in spring.

highlights.title: An original frame
highlights.text: Wikipedia notes that the building keeps its original structure while similar ones in Sikkim have burned. Look at the wooden pillars, beams and roof from outside and inside, and keep your hands off carved timber.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps to Mangan pass Phodong, and from there Labrang is about 2 km uphill. A local taxi from Phodong costs a few hundred rupees, indicative, or you can walk up in 45 minutes to an hour. Ask about the return before you go.

A reserved small car from Gangtok takes 1.5 to 2 hours for about 40 km, with the last 2 km a steep, narrow road above Phodong. A day loop with Kabi Lungchok and Phodong is about ₹3,000 to 4,500, indicative.
Go to Gangtok first, 4.5 to 5 hours on NH10 from either, longer via Kalimpong or Algarah when NH10 is closed by slides. Visit Labrang on a day trip from Gangtok or on your way north.

costs: Phodong to Labrang by local taxi
Free or a small donation, as far as we know
where_to_stay: We do not plan nights at Labrang. Most visitors see it on a day trip from Gangtok with Phodong and Kabi Lungchok. If you want to stay nearby, ask us about small lodges and homestays in the Phodong area, whose availability varies. Mangan, about 29 km further north, has simple hotels, and Gangtok has the widest choice, with budget rooms around ₹1,500 to 3,000 a night and better hotels above that.
tips: Visit Phodong first and drive or walk up to Labrang afterwards, as the road is short and steep.
Carry a warm layer, because the ledge at about 2,130 m is cool and often misty.
Remove shoes and hats before the hall, and ask before taking photographs.
Wear shoes with grip for the lane, which can be slippery after rain.
Check ahead if you want to see the museum, as opening hours depend on the monastery.

experiences.title: Visiting Labrang Monastery
experiences.summary: A quiet hour at a Nyingma monastery built between 1826 and 1843, on a forest ledge above Phodong. See the courtyard, prayer hall and statues, and understand why Labrang feels very different from its Kagyu neighbour below.
body: Labrang is smaller and quieter than Phodong, and the approach is steep, narrow and tree-lined. At the top, a flat ledge holds the monastery. Wikipedia records its construction from 1826 to 1843, with Gyalshe Rigzing Chempa as founder, in memory of Lhatsun Chempo. The building feels older and more weathered than many Sikkim monasteries.

Leave shoes and hat outside and enter quietly. Inside you may see statues, wall paintings and a bronze figure of Karma Guru, a wrathful form of Padmasambhava. Ask before taking photographs, and do not touch objects. A donation box is usual, and a small offering is a good way to say thank you.

Allow an hour, more if the museum is open. The ledge is cool even in spring, so carry a jacket. Mist can close in by mid-afternoon, so go in the morning. Hours and any fees are the monastery's decision, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What school does Labrang Monastery belong to?
faqs.a: Labrang is a Nyingma monastery, belonging to the oldest school of Tibetan Buddhism. Phodong Monastery below it is Karma Kagyu, so visiting both lets you compare two traditions in a morning. Wikipedia lists Labrang among Nyingma monasteries in Sikkim.

faqs.q: How long does a visit take?
faqs.a: Allow about an hour for the hall and courtyard, and up to 90 minutes if the museum is open and you want to look at the objects. With Phodong Monastery below it, plan a two-hour monastery stop. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Labrang?
faqs.a: As far as we know there is no fixed ticket, and visitors usually leave a small donation. Fees and rules for photography can change, so check current status before you travel and follow the caretaker's advice.

experiences.title: Looking at Labrang's statues, texts and murals
experiences.image_query: Labrang Monastery museum Buddha statues Sikkim
experiences.summary: Spend time in Labrang's museum and prayer hall, where Wikipedia records a large collection of Buddha statues, sutras and murals, and a bronze statue of Karma Guru. A short, close look at Tibetan Buddhist art in Sikkim.
body: Wikipedia's article says the monastery houses a museum with a large collection of Buddha statues, sutras and murals. The museum is small, and opening hours depend on the monastery, so ask at the gate. If it is closed, the prayer hall holds statues and paintings that are worth the stop.

Look at how each figure is painted and posed: hands, colours and what the figure holds. A caretaker or monk may explain a few of them if you ask politely. The bronze Karma Guru is a wrathful form of Padmasambhava, and Wikipedia lists it among the notable objects.

Do not touch statues, murals or books, and do not photograph inside unless permitted. Keep to the path and speak quietly. If you are interested in texts, remember that sutras are sacred objects, not display pieces. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a museum at Labrang?
faqs.a: Wikipedia says the monastery houses a museum with a large collection of Buddha statues, sutras and murals. Opening hours depend on the monastery and visits may need a caretaker to unlock it. Check current status before you travel and ask at the gate.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Labrang?
faqs.a: Ask first. Many Sikkim monasteries allow photography in the courtyard but not inside the prayer hall or museum, and some charge a fee. Follow any sign and the caretaker's advice, and never use flash near murals or statues.

faqs.q: What is Karma Guru?
faqs.a: Karma Guru is a wrathful form of Padmasambhava, the teacher honoured in the Nyingma school as bringing Buddhism to Tibet. Wikipedia records a bronze statue of it at Labrang. If you want to understand the form, ask a monk politely, and do not touch the statue.

experiences.title: Walking up from Phodong to Labrang
experiences.summary: Walk the steep 2 km lane from Phodong up to Labrang through forest, with the option of taking a car back. A modest climb, best done in the morning in clear weather, with birdsong and views over terraced slopes.
body: The lane from Phodong to Labrang is about 2 km and climbs several hundred metres, from roughly 1,400 m to about 2,130 m by our approximate figures. Allow 45 minutes to an hour uphill and 30 minutes down. The road is narrow, and a few vehicles use it, so keep to the edge and listen at bends.

Wear shoes with grip, carry water and a rain jacket, and start before 10 am. The forest around Labrang is dense and the afternoon mist can close in. Pace yourself: the altitude is modest, but the climb is steady, and older walkers may prefer to drive up and walk down.

Avoid the walk in heavy rain, when the lane is slippery and slides are possible, and during the June to September monsoon. Leave no litter, do not pick plants and ask before photographing people. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How steep is the walk to Labrang?
faqs.a: It is steady and steep in places, about 2 km uphill from Phodong, climbing several hundred metres. Most fit walkers take 45 minutes to an hour. If you are unsure, drive up and walk down. Wear shoes with grip and carry water. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the lane safe to walk?
faqs.a: By day in dry weather, yes, with care. It is a narrow road shared with a few vehicles, so keep to the edge and take care at bends. Avoid it in heavy rain or mist, and tell your driver or hotel about your plan.

faqs.q: Can I get a taxi from Phodong to Labrang?
faqs.a: Local taxis usually run between Phodong and Labrang for a few hundred rupees, indicative, and your own car can do the same. Ask in the bazaar. Fares are negotiable and may change, so ask before you get in and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Two monasteries in one morning
experiences.summary: Visit Phodong Monastery, a Karma Kagyu house credited to 1740, and Labrang, a Nyingma monastery built 1826 to 1843, in one outing. The pairing shows two Tibetan Buddhist traditions within 2 km of each other.
body: Start at Phodong Monastery in the early morning, when the courtyard is quiet. Walk around the main hall and the monks' quarters, then drive or walk the 2 km up to Labrang. Phodong is Karma Kagyu, with a founding credited to Chogyal Gyurmed Namgyal in 1740 on Wikipedia's infobox. Labrang is Nyingma and later, with its construction dated 1826 to 1843.

Compare what you see. Phodong's courtyard is wide and public, the setting of the December chaam. Labrang is smaller, with a museum, a bronze Karma Guru and a timber building that keeps its original frame. The forest around Labrang is cooler and quieter than the town below.

Allow three to four hours with a stop for tea in the Phodong bazaar. A small car for the day from Gangtok, with Kabi Lungchok on the way, costs about ₹3,000 to 4,500, indicative. Check current status before you travel and ask about the monasteries' opening hours.

faqs.q: Can I visit both monasteries in one morning?
faqs.a: Yes. They are about 2 km apart, so you can see Phodong and then Labrang in three to four hours including stops. Start early, as Labrang can be misty in the afternoon, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which is better, Phodong or Labrang?
faqs.a: Phodong is the larger, better known, and the setting of the December chaam. Labrang is quieter, with a museum and a forest setting. We would not choose between them: the visit works best as a pair, and the two belong to different schools.

faqs.q: What is the best order for visiting?
faqs.a: Visit Phodong first, in the morning, then drive up to Labrang. This keeps the steep lane for later when you are warm, and puts the quieter monastery at the end. If you are coming for the chaam in December, spend most of the day at Phodong.

faqs.q: Where is Labrang Monastery?
faqs.a: Labrang Monastery is about 2 km above Phodong Monastery, 38 km from Gangtok, in Mangan district (North Sikkim). It sits on flat ground on a forested hill, reached by a short, steep road from Phodong.

faqs.q: How old is Labrang Monastery?
faqs.a: Wikipedia records that Labrang was built from 1826 to 1843 by Gyalshe Rigzing Chempa, a son of Chogyal Tsugphud Namgyal, and renovated in 1978 with government aid. It was damaged in the 2006 earthquake. We give these dates as recorded there.

faqs.q: What school does Labrang belong to?
faqs.a: Labrang is a Nyingma monastery. It is also known as Palden Phuntshog Phodrang. Phodong Monastery, 2 km below it, belongs to the Karma Kagyu school, so visiting both shows two Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Labrang?
faqs.a: Sikkim Tourism gives the altitude as about 7,000 ft, or roughly 2,130 m. That is noticeably cooler than Phodong town, which we put at about 1,400 m, so carry a warm layer even in spring.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Labrang?
faqs.a: No protected area permit is needed for Indian visitors, as Labrang is below the Toong check post. Foreign nationals need the online Sikkim restricted area permit. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is at Labrang Monastery?
faqs.a: A prayer hall with statues and murals, a museum with a large collection of Buddha statues and sutras, and a bronze statue of Karma Guru, a wrathful form of Padmasambhava. The timber building is reported to retain its original structure. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Labrang?
faqs.a: As far as we know no fixed ticket is charged, but a donation is customary and photography in the hall may be restricted. Arrangements can change, so check current status before you travel and carry small notes.

faqs.q: How far is Labrang from Phodong?
faqs.a: About 2 km uphill by a steep, narrow road, roughly 10 minutes by car or 45 minutes to an hour on foot. Local taxis may run the stretch. Check current status before you travel, and avoid the lane in heavy rain.

faqs.q: How much time should we allow?
faqs.a: About an hour at Labrang, plus the time at Phodong Monastery below, so two to three hours for both. Add an hour if you walk up from Phodong. With Kabi Lungchok on the way, a day loop from Gangtok takes six to eight hours.
